items.lead: The tennis board shows the whole day
items.text: Tapping the tennis card now lists up to 26 matches in two columns, each with its round in the draw, instead of eight.

The Microsoft 365 row reported a problem almost permanently, because Microsoft keeps a standing backlog of long-running minor advisories and the board treated them like live outages. Only real incidents color the row now. The advisories are still there under their own heading when you tap the card, with the date each one opened.

items.lead: Cloud Services can be made taller
items.text: The card would not grow past the height needed for the number of services you follow, which was too short whenever one of them had a bad day and printed several lines. You can drag it taller now, and the size sticks.

items.lead: The board comes back at the right size
items.text: A board could come back zoomed in after a restart or after saving a change, showing a corner of the dashboard blown up until someone woke the screen and let it go back to sleep. It comes back at the right size now.
The dashboard is now idlescreen, at idlescreen.app. Every old address keeps working; nothing to do.

The weather service runs routine communications tests, and this morning one of them read as a real tsunami warning on the weather card: the feed marks a drill in a field the banner never showed, so the board repeated it with a straight face. The card now banners only warnings marked as actual, so tests, exercises and cancellation notices stay off the glass.

items.lead: No more broken-picture flash at startup
items.text: Cards that show pictures used to flash a broken-image icon for a second when the board started up, before the real photo appeared. That flash is gone: a picture now either shows finished or not at all, and if one ever fails to load the card quietly keeps what it was showing and tries again on the next refresh.

items.lead: The screen cannot be zoomed by accident
items.text: Pinching the board with two fingers used to blow the dashboard up, and it stayed that way. Even reloading did not clear it, so a board could be left sitting at double size until someone stood in front of it and pinched it back. The board now ignores the gesture entirely. Swiping through pictures, scrolling a long list, and dragging and resizing cards in Edit mode all work exactly as they did.

Tap almost any card holding more than it shows and it opens the full picture, centered where a person standing at the board can see all of it: weather, the pictures, the train boards, markets, subway status and This Day in History; headlines and posts as a reading list you can tap into story by story; cloud services and TfL as a status ledger with the whole incident text; your teams with their latest and next games, the golf and tennis boards, every Citi Bike station, your bus stops counting down live, and the world clock as the same analog faces the screensaver shows. Not every card has somewhere to go, so it is worth a try rather than a rule. When a card is holding back more than it can show, a plain count in its bottom corner says how much more it has. Every card says it the same way, so you can read the whole board at a glance. Picture cards take a tap anywhere on the card now, not only on the picture itself.

Tap the card and the whole season opens across the board. The next Grand Prix leads with the circuit drawn out and the weekend's sessions listed in your own time, counting down to lights out. Beside it the last race sits in full: every driver from the winner's time down to the retirements, with where each one started, what they scored, and the fastest lap of the race picked out. Both championships run down the far side, the drivers with their win counts and every constructor with its points.
The card fits a smaller space now. Three cities read clearly on a short, wide one, so a world clock can sit along the bottom of the board instead of claiming a taller card. Resize it in Edit mode.

When a provider has several things wrong at once, the card now names each affected piece on its own line, right on the dashboard. A bad Microsoft morning reads as Exchange, Teams and the suite one under the other, instead of one line standing in for all three. Services that are fine give up the room, and anything pushed off the card is counted in the corner as always.

The Microsoft row is telling the truth again. The page it used to read from was retired, so the row had quietly been saying status unavailable to everyone walking past. It reads Microsoft's own status pages now, and it finally covers the Microsoft an office actually uses: when Exchange mail, Teams, SharePoint or OneDrive is having a bad morning, the board says which one and shows the details behind a tap. Back office things like Defender and Purview are listed there too, without turning the whole row amber on their own. If only one of the two pages answers, the row reports what that one knows instead of going blank.

Adding, removing and resizing cards all happen in one place now: Edit mode, on the dashboard itself, where you can see what fits as you go. The Widgets page hands you straight there with a single button, and anything you changed elsewhere in Settings is saved on the way.
The card now chooses a saying that fits it, so a quote is never cut off in the middle of its own point. A small card reads a shorter quote; a wide one still gets the long ones.
When an alert names another line partway through a sentence, the card now draws that line's coloured bullet instead of its letter in brackets. Same on the full status board behind a tap.
Tap anywhere on the card for the whole day: every event at reading size, oldest first. The corner shows how many more the day holds beyond what the card fits.

Swiping a photo, in a full screen view or on the screensaver including the clock backdrop, now dims calmly to black the moment you swipe and rises on the next photo, the same way the screensaver first appears. The automatic rotation keeps its slow dissolve, and the next photos load ahead of your swipe so nothing hesitates.

Sports headlines on the board, merged newest first from ESPN, CBS Sports, Yahoo Sports and The Athletic, with BBC Sport and Guardian Sport there if you want them. Narrow it to particular sports with the chips in Settings, or flip on Only my teams to read your teams' league sections and see just their stories. Find it under Sports.
When several outlets cover the same story, your cards now show it once, in its freshest telling. This covers Headlines, Markets News and Sports News.

When a departure card holds more than it can show, a small +N more sits in its corner. Tap the card for the full board: every departure it knows about, large and centered, with lines and tracks. It closes on its own after a minute, like the other full screen views.
Notices about a single station, like an elevator outage or a closed entrance, now show only when that station is one of yours. Line-wide service alerts still reach everyone riding the line.
Tap an alert banner to read the whole notice full screen, including details the card cannot fit. Tapping anywhere else on the card still opens the departure board.

The card now lists trains beyond the next two hours, so a quiet evening shows tonight's later departures instead of stopping short. Cards carrying an alert also fit their trains more honestly, without giving up extra room.

LIRR and Metro-North cards now show only the alerts that could affect your ride: your branch, your stations, or the whole railroad. Notices about other lines no longer take up a row your departures could use.
Track numbers now appear the moment the railroad posts them, the same as the boards in the station. The card no longer shows the planned track, which could differ from the one finally assigned.
A departure far in the future no longer pushes its row out of line with the others: the countdown column simply makes room for the wider number.
A status source that stumbles now gets a couple of quick retries before the card calls it Unknown, so a brief blip at the provider no longer reads as missing status.

You can now put your tickers in the order you want. Drag a ticker by the arrows on the left of its row, and the list shows a line across it: everything above the line is on the card now, and everything below it is one tap away. Reordering also takes effect straight away instead of waiting a few minutes.

The screensaver now fills the whole display. Photos and artwork are no longer trimmed off at the bottom edge, and the title and artist line sits clear of the information band instead of half behind it. On a Room Navigator the black strip under the picture is gone.
Photos now fade gently from one to the next instead of drawing in from the top of the card. The same calm change covers Landscapes, Art and the daily NASA photo.

The add menu is grouped more clearly. World Clock and Cloud Services now sit together under Reference, and the daily reads have their own Daily group: This Day in History, Quote of the Day, Word of the Day and Chart of the Day.
You can now read what is new on the board itself: open the gear and tap What’s new at the bottom of the settings list. The board also shows which version it is running.

Tap a card for its full screen view and the close hint now sits well clear of the data instead of crowding it. Tapping a Landscapes photo fills the whole display too, the way the screensaver already showed it, rather than leaving black bars down the sides.
Sports and image widgets now sit in their own groups in the add menu, tucked behind a tap like Commute, so the list stays short.

New Surf card: water temperature, wave height and period, and whether the wind is helping, for the water near your board's location. Tap it for the 48 hour picture. It only shows up in the widget list when your board is near a coast.
Updates now apply without the screen flashing white for a moment.
Services having an outage now rise to the top of the card, so a problem is visible even when your list is longer than the card.
Tap the Weather card for the full picture: 24 hours of temperature and rain, a 7 day outlook, wind, humidity, UV, and sunrise and sunset times.
Tap the Markets card to see every ticker you follow, full screen. It closes by itself after a minute. And you can now follow up to 20 tickers, up from 10.

Tap the Subway card to see every line at once. The lines running normally collapse into a single row of badges, and every line with a problem shows its full alert, including the details the card has to cut short.
LIRR, Metro-North, and NJ Transit departures now show each train’s line as a colored badge in its official line colors, so the line is easy to tell apart from the destination.
Train and ferry cards now fit more departures in the same space, so bigger cards show more of what is coming next.
Every hour now shows its chance of rain, marked with a small droplet. Tall weather cards draw a bigger temperature curve, and calm nights read calm.
If an update ever goes wrong, the display explains what happened, keeps retrying, and recovers on its own instead of going dark.
Tap any post to read it full screen, with a QR code to keep reading on your phone. Cards also fill their space with more posts.
Departures now stay accurate all day.
The dashboard automatically fits companion panels like the Cisco Room Navigator. No more pinch to zoom.
Tap a headline for its summary and a QR code to the full article. The board itself never navigates away.
Sparklines and the temperature trend draw as smooth curves, tinted by the day’s direction.
A sharper, recurated vocabulary.
A curated scenery collection, available as a screensaver or a dashboard card.
An optional daily photo backdrop behind the clock faces. Swipe to see the next one.
A dedicated settings page and three full-screen clock faces.
Golf (PGA) and Tennis leaderboards.
Tap any unconfigured card to jump straight to its settings.
Shows your next game after a final instead of going quiet.
Split into iCloud and Google Drive widgets, each with a guided phone setup.
Grand Central support, and departures stay live even when the MTA’s data feed stalls.
Markets, Subway and others fit more at every size.
The Momentum theme became the board’s look. Pure black, calmer type, quieter color.
Choose 12-hour or 24-hour time everywhere.
NJ Transit, PATH, World Clock and Chart of the Day.
Amtrak departures from Moynihan Train Hall, and Formula 1.
The first two weeks built the board itself: more than 25 widgets, phone setup at roomboard.app/setup, screensavers, and setup codes.
